claim: In vertebrates with elongated auditory organs, mechanosensory hair cells (HCs) are organised such that complex sounds are broken down into their component frequencies along a proximal-to-distal long (tonotopic) axis.
source: In vertebrates with elongated auditory organs, mechanosensory hair cells (HCs) are organised such that complex sounds are broken down into their component frequencies along a proximal-to-distal long (tonotopic) axis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about auditory system organization in vertebrates.

claim: There is a gradient in the cellular balance between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway in developing HCs along the tonotopic axis.
source: Using a combination of live imaging and NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy, we reveal that there is a gradient in the cellular balance between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway in developing HCs along the tonotopic axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by NAD(P)H FLIM data presented in the manuscript showing differences in τbound along the tonotopic axis.

claim: Perturbing the balance between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway by inhibiting different branches of cytosolic glucose catabolism disrupts developmental morphogen signalling.
source: Perturbing this balance by inhibiting different branches of cytosolic glucose catabolism disrupts developmental morphogen signalling and abolishes the normal tonotopic gradient in HC morphology.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using metabolic inhibitors (2-DOG, 6-AN, etc.) and their effects on HC morphology and morphogen expression.

claim: Perturbing the balance between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway abolishes the normal tonotopic gradient in HC morphology.
source: Perturbing this balance by inhibiting different branches of cytosolic glucose catabolism disrupts developmental morphogen signalling and abolishes the normal tonotopic gradient in HC morphology.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric data showing loss of HC size gradients after metabolic inhibition.

claim: There is a causal link between graded morphogen signalling and metabolic reprogramming in specifying the tonotopic identity of developing HCs.
source: These findings highlight a causal link between graded morphogen signalling and metabolic reprogramming in specifying the tonotopic identity of developing HCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that metabolic perturbation affects morphogen expression and that Chdl1 can rescue metabolic inhibition effects.

claim: High-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to ageing.
source: As high-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to insults, including ageing (Gordon-Salant, 2005), noise damage (Fettiplace and Nam, 2019; Wu et al., 2020), and ototoxicity (Forge and Richardson, 1993), awareness of the mechanisms underlying the formation of frequency-specific HC properties is crucial to understanding both acquired auditory defects, HC repair and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gordon-Salant, 2005.

claim: High-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to noise damage.
source: As high-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to insults, including ageing (Gordon-Salant, 2005), noise damage (Fettiplace and Nam, 2019; Wu et al., 2020), and ototoxicity (Forge and Richardson, 1993), awareness of the mechanisms underlying the formation of frequency-specific HC properties is crucial to understanding both acquired auditory defects, HC repair and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fettiplace and Nam, 2019; Wu et al., 2020.

claim: High-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to ototoxicity.
source: As high-frequency HCs show increased vulnerability to insults, including ageing (Gordon-Salant, 2005), noise damage (Fettiplace and Nam, 2019; Wu et al., 2020), and ototoxicity (Forge and Richardson, 1993), awareness of the mechanisms underlying the formation of frequency-specific HC properties is crucial to understanding both acquired auditory defects, HC repair and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Forge and Richardson, 1993.

claim: Metabolism has emerged as a key regulator of cell fate and differentiation.
source: Metabolism, encompassing the complex network of chemical reactions that sustain life (summarised in Figure 1), has emerged as a key regulator of cell fate and differentiation (Ito and Ito, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ito and Ito, 2016.

claim: Reciprocity between metabolic networks and the epigenome has been extensively studied in models of cancer cell biology and tumourigenesis.
source: Reciprocity between metabolic networks and the epigenome has been extensively studied in models of cancer cell biology and tumourigenesis (Kinnaird et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kinnaird et al., 2016.

claim: Chromatin modifying enzymes that drive cell fate switches rely upon metabolic intermediates as cofactors or substrates.
source: Here, chromatin modifying enzymes (involved in histone acetylation and methylation) that drive cell fate switches rely upon metabolic intermediates as cofactors or substrates, highlighting a link between cell metabolism and transcriptional regulation (Campbell and Wellen, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Campbell and Wellen, 2018.

claim: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has been reported in migratory neural crest cells.
source: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has also been reported in developing tissues, including migratory neural crest cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2020), the zebrafish otic vesicle (Kantarci et al., 2020), trophectoderm in the mouse embryo (Chi et al., 2020), and the presomitic mesoderm (Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2020.

claim: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has been reported in the zebrafish otic vesicle.
source: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has also been reported in developing tissues, including migratory neural crest cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2020), the zebrafish otic vesicle (Kantarci et al., 2020), trophectoderm in the mouse embryo (Chi et al., 2020), and the presomitic mesoderm (Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kantarci et al., 2020.

claim: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has been reported in trophectoderm in the mouse embryo.
source: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has also been reported in developing tissues, including migratory neural crest cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2020), the zebrafish otic vesicle (Kantarci et al., 2020), trophectoderm in the mouse embryo (Chi et al., 2020), and the presomitic mesoderm (Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chi et al., 2020.

claim: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has been reported in the presomitic mesoderm.
source: Reprogramming between glycolytic and oxidative pathways has also been reported in developing tissues, including migratory neural crest cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2020), the zebrafish otic vesicle (Kantarci et al., 2020), trophectoderm in the mouse embryo (Chi et al., 2020), and the presomitic mesoderm (Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022.

claim: A regulatory role for metabolism has not been explored in the context of cell fate and patterning in the developing inner ear epithelia.
source: Nevertheless, a regulatory role for metabolism has not been explored in the context of cell fate and patterning in the developing inner ear epithelia.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FLIM provides a label-free method to identify metabolic differences between inner ear cell types.
source: We have previously demonstrated that fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides a label-free method to identify metabolic differences between inner ear cell types (Blacker et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Blacker et al., 2014.

claim: NAD(P)H FLIM typically resolves two fluorescence lifetime components in live cells and tissues: one with a duration of around 0.4 ns from freely diffusing NAD(P)H (τfree) and another of 2 ns or more from NAD(P)H bound to enzymes and cofactors (τbound).
source: NAD(P)H FLIM typically resolves two fluorescence lifetime components in live cells and tissues one with a duration of around 0.4 ns coming from freely diffusing NAD(P)H (τfree) and the other of 2 ns or more from the pool of NAD(P)H that is bound to enzymes and cofactors (τbound) (Skala et al., 2007; Yu and Heikal, 2009; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Skala et al., 2007; Yu and Heikal, 2009 and Figure 2B.

claim: Changes in the duration of τbound indicate switching in the enzyme families that are bound to the overall NAD(P)H population.
source: Changes in the duration of τbound indicate switching in the enzyme families that are bound to the overall NAD(P)H population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of NAD(P)H FLIM data based on established understanding of the technique.

claim: A gradient in τbound was observed throughout BP development, specifically at E6 and E9.
source: The gradient observed in τbound throughout BP development, specifically at E6 and E9, is consistent with our previous work, where we showed that graded morphogen signalling along the BP establishes HC positional identity between E6 and E8 (Mann et al., 2014; Thiede et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and citations to Mann et al., 2014; Thiede et al., 2014.

claim: Around E6, when cells in the BP begin acquiring their positional identity, a significant difference in τbound was observed along the tonotopic axis.
source: Around E6, when cells in the BP begin acquiring their positional identity (Mann et al., 2014; Thiede et al., 2014), we observed a significant difference in τbound along the tonotopic axis (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2D-H and citations to Mann et al., 2014; Thiede et al., 2014.

claim: The proximal-to-distal gradient in τbound was evident at E9, when a majority of cells are post mitotic.
source: The proximal-to-distal gradient in τbound (Figure 2D) was also evident at E9, when a majority of cells are post mitotic (Katayama and Corwin, 1989), and at E14, when HCs functionally resemble those in a mature BP (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2D-F and citation to Katayama and Corwin, 1989.

claim: The proximal-to-distal gradient in τbound was evident at E14, when HCs functionally resemble those in a mature BP.
source: The proximal-to-distal gradient in τbound (Figure 2D) was also evident at E9, when a majority of cells are post mitotic (Katayama and Corwin, 1989), and at E14, when HCs functionally resemble those in a mature BP (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Changes in τbound report shifts in the cellular balance between NADPH and NADH.
source: Changes in τbound report shifts in the cellular balance between NADPH and NADH (Blacker et al., 2014; Blacker et al., 2013; Gafni and Brand, 1976), which reflects glucose catabolism in distinct branches of glycolysis (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blacker et al., 2014; Blacker et al., 2013; Gafni and Brand, 1976 and Figure 2H.

claim: TMRM fluorescence revealed no significant difference in ΔΨmt between proximal and distal regions at any developmental stage.
source: TMRM fluorescence revealed no significant difference in ΔΨmt between proximal and distal regions at any developmental stage (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Analysis of TMRM fluorescence revealed a consistently higher ΔΨmt in fully differentiated HCs compared to SCs from E14 onwards.
source: Analysis of TMRM fluorescence revealed a consistently higher ΔΨmt in fully differentiated HCs compared to SCs from E14 onwards (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no significant difference in mitochondrial activity along the tonotopic axis throughout development.
source: These findings indicate no significant difference in mitochondrial activity along the tonotopic axis throughout development, suggesting that the gradient in NADPH/NADH reported by τbound (Figure 2C–G) does not arise from variations in the balance between cytosolic and mitochondrial ATP production, as often observed in development (Bhattacharya et al., 2021) but from differences in the specific route utilised for the processing of glucose in the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is supported by TMRM data in Figure 3 and citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2021.

claim: The gradient in NADPH/NADH does not arise from variations in the balance between cytosolic and mitochondrial ATP production.
source: These findings indicate no significant difference in mitochondrial activity along the tonotopic axis throughout development, suggesting that the gradient in NADPH/NADH reported by τbound (Figure 2C–G) does not arise from variations in the balance between cytosolic and mitochondrial ATP production, as often observed in development (Bhattacharya et al., 2021) but from differences in the specific route utilised for the processing of glucose in the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is inferred from TMRM data showing no tonotopic differences in mitochondrial activity.

claim: 2-NDBG fluorescence analyses revealed no differences in glucose uptake along the tonotopic axis at any developmental stage or between cell types.
source: These analyses revealed no differences in glucose uptake along the tonotopic axis at any developmental stage or between cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C), suggesting differences in the fate rather than overall flux of glucose underpin the gradient in τbound (i.e., NADPH/NADH).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Differences in the fate rather than overall flux of glucose underpin the gradient in τbound.
source: These analyses revealed no differences in glucose uptake along the tonotopic axis at any developmental stage or between cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C), suggesting differences in the fate rather than overall flux of glucose underpin the gradient in τbound (i.e., NADPH/NADH).
evidence: The claim is inferred from 2-NBDG data showing no differences in glucose uptake.

claim: Pyruvate kinase M2 (Pkm2) is the only enzyme linked with cytosolic glucose flux and cellular NADPH/NADH showing consistent differential expression throughout development.
source: From the combined data sets, we identified multiple genes involved in NADPH-linked glucose metabolism with differential expression along the tonotopic axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A). Expression of these genes was verified using RNA scope and Immunohistochemistry. The only enzyme linked with cytosolic glucose flux and cellular NADPH/NADH showing a consistent differential expression throughout development, using all three validation methods, was pyruvate kinase M2 (Pkm2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq, microarray, RNA scope, and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Pkm2 protein expression is higher in HCs at the proximal compared to distal end of the BP between E9 and E14.
source: Consistent with the observed gradient in NAD(P)H (Figure 2) and in Pkm2 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3), we show higher Pkm2 protein expression in HCs but not SCs at the proximal compared to distal end of the BP between E9 and E14 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: A more alkaline pHi was identified in HCs at the proximal compared to distal end of the organ at E9.
source: We identified opposing proximal-to-distal gradients in pHi in HCs and SCs along the tonotopic axis, using pHrodo Red, which reported a more alkaline pHi in HCs at the proximal compared to distal end of the organ (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by pHrodo Red data in Figure 5.

claim: The higher pHi in the proximal region reflects a metabolic phenotype consistent with higher PPP activity and dimeric Pkm2.
source: The higher pHi in the proximal region reflects a metabolic phenotype consistent with higher PPP activity and dimeric Pkm2.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on known relationships between pH, PPP activity, and Pkm2 conformation.

claim: At E14, the pH gradients are reversed compared to E9.
source: To investigate whether the proximal-to-distal gradient in pH was maintained at later developmental stages, we also quantified the pHrodo Red signal in HCs and SCs at E14. At later developmental stages, we find the pH gradients to be reversed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tonotopic patterning and positional identity are specified between E6 and E7.5.
source: As tonotopic patterning and positional identity are specified between E6 and E7.5 (Mann et al., 2014), the gradient at E14 is unlikely to impact the gradient in HC morphology.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mann et al., 2014.

claim: In control cultures, HCs developed with normal tonotopic morphologies.
source: In control cultures, HCs developed with the normal tonotopic morphologies (lumenal surface area, nuclear size and gross bundle morphology) (Figure 6A, C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6A, C, D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When glucose catabolism was blocked between E6.5 and E13.5 equivalent, tonotopic patterning was abolished.
source: In contrast, when glucose catabolism was blocked between E6.5 and E13.5 equivalent, tonotopic patterning was abolished. This was indicated by a uniformly more distal-like HC phenotype along the BP (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6A-B showing effects of 2-DOG treatment.

claim: Treatment with 2-DOG caused a significant increase in HC density in the proximal but not distal BP region.
source: In addition to changes in HC morphology, treatment with 2-DOG caused a significant increase in HC density in the proximal but not distal BP region (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, C) again consistent with loss of tonotopic patterning along the organ.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, C.

claim: A consistent reduction in proliferation throughout the whole explant was observed when glucose metabolism was blocked with 2-DOG.
source: We observed a consistent reduction in proliferation throughout the whole explant when glucose metabolism was blocked with 2-DOG (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, D.

claim: Reciprocal morphogen gradients of Bmp7 and Chdl1 establish HC positional identity at the morphological level along the developing BP between E6.5 and E8.
source: As shown in our previous work, reciprocal morphogen gradients of Bmp7 and Chdl1 establish HC positional identity at the morphological level along the developing BP between E6.5 and E8 (Mann et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mann et al., 2014.

claim: The gradient in HC morphology developed normally in BPs treated with 2-DOG for 24 hr but was absent in those treated for 48 hr.
source: The gradient in HC morphology developed normally in BPs treated with 2-DOG for 24 hr but was absent in those treated for 48 hr (Figure 6C–D, Figure 7A & C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6C-D and Figure 7A, C, D.

claim: Glucose metabolism acts within the same developmental time window as Bmp7 and Chdl1 to set up tonotopic patterning along the BP.
source: These results suggest that glucose metabolism acts within the same developmental time window as Bmp7 and Chdl1 to set up tonotopic patterning along the BP.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-DOG time-course experiments showing effects between 24-48 hours.

claim: Treatment of explants with 6-AN caused a significant reduction in proximal compared to distal hair cell lumenal surface area.
source: Treatment of explants with 6-AN, a specific blocker of flux through the pentose phosphate pathway, caused a significant reduction in proximal compared to distal hair cell lumenal surface area.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 7C showing effects of 6-AN treatment.

claim: Blocking glycolysis at the level of PFK between E6.5 and E13.5 had no effect on HC morphology along the tonotopic axis.
source: Blocking glycolysis at the level of PFK between E6.5 and E13.5 had no effect on HC morphology along the tonotopic axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing effects of YZ9 treatment.

claim: Tonotopic patterning is regulated by glucose flux in the upper branch of glycolysis, rather than by enzymes in the lower branch of the pathway.
source: Therefore, whilst blocking glycolysis and the PPP elicited significant changes in the cell size, disrupting the downstream branches of glycolysis while leaving PPP flux intact had no effect (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Source data 1 and Source data 2). Consistent with a higher NADPH/NADH ratio these findings suggest that tonotopic patterning is regulated by glucose flux in the upper branch of glycolysis, rather than by enzymes in the lower branch of the pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing effects of different metabolic inhibitors shown in Figure 7 and supplements.

claim: Treatment of explants with shikonin during HC formation abolished the normal tonotopic gradient in HC lumenal surface area.
source: Treatment of explants with shikonin during HC formation abolished the normal tonotopic gradient in HC lumenal surface area (Figure 8A, C), where HC cuticular plate circumference was significantly increased in the distal but not proximal BP region compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 8A, C showing effects of shikonin treatment.

claim: Absence of Pkm2 activity did not alter HC nuclear area.
source: Absence of Pkm2 activity did not alter HC nuclear area (Figure 8D), suggesting that the enzyme could play a more important role regulating HC morphology and patterning at the epithelial surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 8D.

claim: Blocking both PPP and Pkm2 pathways during development abolished the normal gradient in HC morphology along the tonotopic axis.
source: We find that blocking both pathways during development abolished the normal gradient in HC morphology along the tonotopic axis, thus mimicking the effects seen when inhibiting glycolysis using 2-DOG (Figure 8A, E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 8A, E, F showing effects of combined shikonin + 6-AN treatment.

claim: Metabolic activity in both PPP and Pkm2 pathways is important for establishing HC positional identity along the developing BP.
source: These data therefore suggest that metabolic activity in both PPP and Pkm2 pathways is important for establishing HC positional identity along the developing BP.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of blocking both pathways.

claim: HCs in explants treated with UK5099 between E6.5 and E13.5 developed with abnormal morphologies at all positions along the BP and displayed either immature stereociliary bundles or lacked them completely.
source: HCs in explants treated with UK5099 between E6.5 and E13.5 developed with abnormal morphologies at all positions along the BP and displayed either immature stereociliary bundles or lacked them completely (Figure 9A, C, red arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 9A, C showing effects of UK5099 treatment.

claim: Pyruvate-mediated OXPHOS plays a more significant role in maintaining the overall progression of development rather than regulating the patterning along the tonotopic axis.
source: However, our findings suggest that pyruvate-mediated OXPHOS plays a more significant role in maintaining the overall progression of development rather than regulating the patterning along the tonotopic axis.
evidence: This is inferred from UK5099 experiments showing global developmental effects rather than tonotopic-specific effects.

claim: Treatment with 2-DOG from E6.5 for 72 hr disrupts the normal tonotopic expression of Bmp7 and its antagonist Chdl1.
source: Treatment of explant cultures with 2-DOG + NaP from E6.5 for 72 hr in vitro disrupts the normal tonotopic expression of Bmp7 and its antagonist Chdl1. Images show in situ hybridisation for Bmp7 and Chdl1 in BP whole-mounts treated with 2-DOG + NaP from E6.5 for 72 hr in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Following treatment with 2-DOG, Bmp7 expression appeared to increase along the entire BP while Chdl1 showed a reciprocal decrease along the length of the organ.
source: Following treatment with 2-DOG, Bmp7 expression appeared to increase along the entire BP while Chdl1 showed a reciprocal decrease along the length of the organ.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Treatment with 6-AN from E6.5 for 72 hr caused marked changes in the expression levels of Bmp7 and Chdl1.
source: Treatment of explant cultures with 6-AN from E6.5 for 72 hr in vitro caused marked changes in the expression levels of Bmp7 and Chdl1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking mitochondrial-linked glucose catabolism with UK5099 did not alter the expression of Bmp7.
source: Blocking mitochondrial-linked glucose catabolism with UK5099 did not alter the expression of Bmp7 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of explants treated between E6.5 and E13.5 equivalent with 2-DOG + 0.4 μg/ml Chdl1 showed a partial rescue of HC morphologies along the proximal-to-distal axis.
source: Analysis of explants treated between E6.5 and E13.5 equivalent with 2-DOG + 0.4 μg/ml Chdl1 showed a partial rescue of HC morphologies (lumenal surface area and nuclear area) along the proximal-to-distal axis (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1, and Source data 1 and Source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 11 and Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: A distinct metabolic state coupled with a specific morphogen level can regulate HC morphology at different positions along the tonotopic axis during development.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that a distinct metabolic state coupled with a specific morphogen level can regulate HC morphology at different positions along the tonotopic axis during development.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from metabolic inhibition and Chdl1 rescue experiments.

claim: The gradient in cellular NADPH originates from differences in glucose flux between high- and low-frequency HCs.
source: We identify a tonotopic gradient in cellular NADPH, originating from differences in glucose flux between high- and low-frequency HCs.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by NAD(P)H FLIM and metabolic inhibitor data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tonotopic differences in the catabolic fate of glucose in glycolysis or the PPP modulates Bmp7 and Chdl-1 signalling along the developing BP.
source: Tonotopic differences in the catabolic fate of glucose in glycolysis or the PPP modulates Bmp7 and Chdl-1 signalling along the developing BP.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by metabolic inhibition experiments and in situ hybridization data.

claim: This study provides the first evidence supporting a role for crosstalk between metabolism and morphogen gradients in the developing auditory system.
source: This study provides the first evidence supporting a role for crosstalk between metabolism and morphogen gradients in the developing auditory system, building on our current understanding of cell fate specification.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the novelty of the findings.

claim: Differences in the fate of cytosolic glucose underpin the increased τbound lifetime and higher NADPH/NADH ratio in high-frequency HCs.
source: Collectively, these analyses indicate that differences in the fate of cytosolic glucose, (Grüning et al., 2011; Yang and Lu, 2015; Alfarouk et al., 2020) rather than between glycolytic and oxidative metabolic states underpin the increased τbound lifetime and higher NADPH/NADH ratio reported here for high-frequency HCs.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings supported by citations to Grüning et al., 2011; Yang and Lu, 2015; Alfarouk et al., 2020.

claim: The higher expression of PKM2 and the more alkaline pH identified in proximal HCs are consistent with a higher cellular NADPH/NADH ratio.
source: The higher expression of PKM2 and the more alkaline pH identified in proximal HCs are also consistent with a higher cellular NADPH/NADH ratio (Nandi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to Nandi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Cell size, cell membrane composition, and metabolic rate are tightly correlated.
source: Cell size, cell membrane composition, and metabolic rate are tightly correlated (Hulbert and Else, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hulbert and Else, 1999.

claim: PPP-derived NADPH is utilised extensively in proliferating cells during development, where it regulates cell cycle progression, differentiation, and growth.
source: PPP-derived NADPH is utilised extensively in proliferating cells during development, where it regulates cell cycle progression, differentiation, and growth (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Vizán et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Vizán et al., 2009.

claim: Increased glucose metabolism has been reported in regenerating and developing systems where it plays an important role in regulating cell fate, behaviour, and shape.
source: Increased glucose metabolism has been reported in regenerating (Love et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022) and developing systems (Chi et al., 2020; Oginuma et al., 2017; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022) where it plays an important role in regulating cell fate, behaviour, and shape.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Love et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2020; Oginuma et al., 2017; Bulusu et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022.

claim: PPP metabolism regulates cell division and proliferation through its ability to generate lipid and nucleotide precursors.
source: PPP metabolism regulates cell division and proliferation through its ability to generate lipid and nucleotide precursors (Stincone et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stincone et al., 2015.

claim: Increased glucose flux into the PPP but not the main branch of glycolysis was shown to regulate the balance between proliferation and cell death in the regenerating limb.
source: Increased glucose flux into the PPP but not the main branch of glycolysis was also recently shown to regulate the balance between proliferation and cell death in the regenerating limb (Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Patel et al., 2022.

claim: In the BP, HCs exit the cell cycle in three progressive waves following a centre-to-periphery progression beginning at E5.
source: In the BP, HCs exit the cell cycle in three progressive waves following a centre-to-periphery progression beginning at E5.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BP development.

claim: During HC cell cycle exit, both HCs and SCs are added in apposition to the edges of the band of post-mitotic cells that preceded them.
source: During this process, both HCs and SCs are added in apposition, to the edges of the band of post-mitotic cells that preceded them (Katayama and Corwin, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Katayama and Corwin, 1989.

claim: HC differentiation begins in the distal portion of the BP at around E6 and extends proximally along the cochlea expanding across the width of the epithelium.
source: HC differentiation then begins in the distal portion of the BP at around E6 and extends proximally along the cochlea expanding across the width of the epithelium (Goodyear and Richardson, 1997; Cotanche and Sulik, 1984; Bartolami et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goodyear and Richardson, 1997; Cotanche and Sulik, 1984; Bartolami et al., 1991.

claim: Graded differences in HC size along the organ are an essential requirement for correct auditory coding.
source: These graded differences in HC size along the organ are an essential requirement for correct auditory coding (Fettiplace and Fuchs, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fettiplace and Fuchs, 1999.

claim: Larger cell size is correlated with increased G6PDH activity and thus more glucose flux into the PPP.
source: As larger cell size is correlated with increased G6PDH activity and thus more glucose flux into the PPP (Vizán et al., 2009), the higher activity in the proximal BP region may underlie the graded differences in HC size that arise during development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vizán et al., 2009.

claim: PPP metabolism is closely linked with de novo synthesis of lipids and cholesterol, which form an integral part of cell membranes.
source: PPP metabolism is also closely linked with de novo synthesis of lipids and cholesterol, which form an integral part of cell membranes (Sykes et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sykes et al., 1986.

claim: Functional interactions between ion channel complexes in the membrane and the local lipid environment have been described in mammalian and avian HCs.
source: Functional interactions between ion channel complexes in the membrane and the local lipid environment have been described previously in mammalian (Hirono et al., 2004; Gianoli et al., 2017) and avian HCs (Purcell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirono et al., 2004; Gianoli et al., 2017; Purcell et al., 2011.

claim: Frequency tuning in the BP relies on the intrinsic electrical properties of the HCs themselves, where graded differences in the number and kinetics of voltage-gated calcium channels and calcium-sensitive (BK type) potassium channels underlie the ability of HCs to resonate electrically in response to sound.
source: Frequency tuning in the BP relies on the intrinsic electrical properties of the HCs themselves, where graded differences in the number and kinetics of voltage-gated calcium channels and calcium-sensitive (BK type) potassium channels underlie the ability of HCs to resonate electrically in response to sound (Fettiplace and Fuchs, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fettiplace and Fuchs, 1999.

claim: The graded PPP activity may regulate aspects of HC electrical tuning by regulating cholesterol in the HC membrane.
source: By regulating cholesterol in the HC membrane, the graded PPP activity observed here may also regulate aspects of HC electrical tuning.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the relationship between PPP, cholesterol synthesis, and HC electrical properties.

claim: Morphogen signalling gradients have well defined roles in directing cell identity along developing axes, where cells determine their fate as a function of morphogen concentrations at different positions along them.
source: Morphogen signalling gradients have well defined roles in directing cell identity along developing axes, where cells determine their fate as a function of morphogen concentrations at different positions along them (Towers et al., 2012; Dessaud et al., 2008; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Towers et al., 2012; Dessaud et al., 2008; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019.

claim: The gradient of Bmp7 is established by Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signalling emanating from ventral midline structures, including the notochord and floor plate.
source: The gradient of Bmp7 is established by Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signalling emanating from ventral midline structures, including the notochord and floor plate (Son et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Son et al., 2015.

claim: Disrupting the metabolic gradient using 2-DOG, SAM, or 6-AN mimics the effects on HC morphology reported for altered Shh and Bmp7 signalling.
source: Disrupting this gradient using 2-DOG, SAM, or 6-AN mimics the effects on HC morphology reported previously for altered Shh (Son et al., 2015) and Bmp7 signalling (Mann et al., 2014), which induced distal-like HC phenotypes in the proximal BP.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of metabolic inhibition data with previous studies cited (Son et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2014).

claim: Metabolic gradients regulate elongation of the body axis and somite patterning.
source: Metabolic gradients are also known to regulate elongation of the body axis and somite patterning (Oginuma et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oginuma et al., 2017; Miyazawa et al., 2022.

claim: By establishing a gradient in intracellular pH, glycolysis drives graded Wnt signalling and specifies mesodermal versus neuronal cell fate along the developing body axis.
source: By establishing a gradient in intracellular pH, glycolysis drives graded Wnt signalling and specifies mesodermal versus neuronal cell fate along the developing body axis (Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oginuma et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2020; Bulusu et al., 2017.
